analysis.investment_thesis: Super Iron fails both legs of the Magic Formula: ROCE of 7.41% is nowhere near the 20%+ threshold for a "good business," and a P/E of 25.4 implies an earnings yield of just ~3.9%, far below the 12% "cheap" bar. This is neither a good business nor a cheap one — a classic pass.
key_strengths: High promoter skin-in-the-game at 70.88% aligns incentives
Established 1988 casting exporter with multi-decade operating history
Small Rs 66 Cr market cap leaves room for re-rating if ROCE improves
key_risks: ROCE of 7.41% barely exceeds cost of capital — capital-destructive at the margin
Earnings yield ~3.9% vs risk-free ~7% in India means negative real spread
Castings & forgings is capital-intensive and cyclical, compressing FCF conversion
red_flags: ROE 6.2% < ROCE 7.4% suggests leverage is not earning its keep
25x P/E on a sub-scale, low-return foundry is unjustified
No evidence of sustained high returns on capital
analysis.detailed_analysis:
On the Magic Formula scorecard, Super Iron ranks poorly on both axes. Return on capital at 7.41% ROCE is roughly a third of what I'd want to see in a "good business" — foundries tie up heavy working capital and fixed assets, and the returns here don't compensate. Simultaneously, a trailing P/E of 25.4 translates to an earnings yield under 4%, which is worse than an Indian government bond. Paying a premium multiple for sub-par returns on capital is the exact opposite of what the formula is built to find.

The only mild positives are high promoter ownership (70.88%) signaling alignment, and a tiny Rs 66 Cr market cap that could move fast if operating leverage kicks in. But those are qualitative sweeteners on a quantitatively weak profile. Until ROCE moves decisively above 15% or the price collapses to produce a double-digit earnings yield, this is a clear avoid under my systematic framework.
